projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Baruch Zamesky was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Baruch Zaremsky. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Zaremsky's home in Cleveland Heights, Ohio, on January 7th, 2003. Mr. Zaremsky was a piano teacher, and at the end of our interview, he wants to play a little something for me, so I have left that on this recording. Baruch was 76 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941? ZAREMSKY: 1941? I was living with my parents at 3572 Sheldon Road, just west of Lee Road in Shaker Heights. At that time this was called Kinsman. Now it's called Chagrin Boulevard.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And were you still in school?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: In 1941? Yes, I was still in school. I graduated Shaker High in 1944.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The day the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Well, I know the day--when you say specific, I mean, I know it was a dastardly thing, but I didn't have any relatives in the service at that time and it's hard for me to remember. I mean, the Jewish people already at that time had been started--the Nazis had started the Holocaust and it's hard to remember. I mean, that age that I would have been, 15 years old. And of course at that time I was involved in Labor Zionist Movement. Labor Zionist Movement being the movement that today would be considered the Labor Alignment in Israel, HaMa'arakh, the party of Yitzhak Rabin, Shimon Peres, the Party of Peace. The youth movement at that time was habooleen (ph), which means in Hebrew "the builders."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have relatives in Europe that were victims of the Holocaust?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Obviously, but I didn't know their names. I didn't know their names. Later on, though, I mean, as a leader of the Labor Zionist Movement in this city, came the Warsaw Ghetto Memorial. Each year the federation sponsors the remembrance of the Holocaust and one time, since I was a leader in the Labor Zionist Movement, I was on the committee to arrange it and there were two movies shown. One of the movies was a very graphic Warsaw Ghetto fighters fighting door-to-door with the Nazis. The other one was a musician, like myself, playing the piano while co-religionists died. So I was in favor of the second one. In other words, I felt that even though as someone who didn't--was not a survivor, I could identify as well as anyone with the survivors. But most of the people on the--on the committee were called disloyal, in other words, there was actual survivors and they wanted blood and guts. They wanted violence depicted and...and...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything--you say you graduated 1944. Do you remember doing anything while you were still in school for the war efforts, scrap drives, whatever?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You weren't involved in much of that during your high school years?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Not in the high school years. Later on in 1948 I became very much involved in the progressive party, namely the party of Henry Welch.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: 19--the end of February, the beginning of March 1945.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What branch of the service was that?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: In the Navy. I went in as a radio tech. Unfortunately, I flunked out of radio school. I was not very good with my hands. I could understand the theory, what's happening with the radios, but as far as building them, I was not very good. And even though I went in in Theodor Herzl Junior College, I went into the Navy after boot camp at Great Lakes from--from--from Theodor Herzl I went to Dearborn, Michigan, where I even had a chief petty officer working with me trying to improve my technique, it didn't work, and I flunked out of the radio school. From there I went to the ABSD No. 5, the advance base sectional dry dock, near Samar in the Philippines. And there I learned to play two-deck pinnacle, and we played a concert in the Navy with a third of the keys missing on the piano and that didn't bother me. And really the experience in the Navy was basically negative, negative meaning I flunked out of radio school. And even though I went into college right after high school, went to Western Reserve premed, the fact that I flunked out of radio school suggested I wouldn't be--me at that time wouldn't be a good doctor, but not necessarily so, but I'd already--had already begun to teach the piano at the age of 18. That was something that I had to do and figured to go to medical school--in other words, on the assumption that because you flunked out of radio school you wouldn't be a good doctor and, A, it cost a lot of money and my father was just an electrician. And so the high school chemistry teacher at Shaker High, Mr. Stager, made it quite interesting for me. So I went into chemistry. And because at that time the Jewish Vocational Service suggested that there was a discrimination against Jews in chemistry, I went and got a doctorate. So it was better to have a chance to get a job. That's the way it worked out. I got a job at Farrell--Farrell Chemical, division of Farrell Corporation, and I stayed there for 44 years. I set a record for service. But the real icing on the cake was that in 1980, after I'd been there for about 27 years, I became the chief volunteer officer, even though without a title. I raised money for United Way, for the March of Dimes Walk America, I was the blood bank chairman, I arranged bloodmobiles, and once a year we have a bloodmobile--we have a luncheon for those who gave blood, and I would get to play the piano.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you part of the Navy band?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You just played the piano when they asked you to?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: No. In the Navy, I mean, the Navy I just--people happened to know that I played. So when I had a chance, I just played. I wasn't part of the band.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of your time when you were training with the Navy?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Absolutely. Absolutely. In boot camp, at Great Lakes in Company 314, we had all kinds of guys in there, and there was this guy, this smart aleck from Harvard University, one time saluted-- the company commander's name was Donald Freeoh (ph), big bull chest and shoulders. Instead of like this, he went like this. So the company commander came up to him and did this. I'll always remember that. The--the-- I think when I got into the ABSD-5, in other words, when I flunked out of Dearborn, Michigan, we were sent overseas. I was in--I was in Detroit on VE Day. I was--I guess it was a great day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you celebrate a lot on that day? Were there a lot of celebrations in Detroit?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: There was a lot of celebrations. I mean, I didn't--I have never been able to handle liquor, so I didn't get drunk or anything like that. As a matter of fact, later on when it was floating in dry dock, some guys on the weekends went to liberty, went to--went to Samar. They came back roaring drunk, and I was-- I was turned off right there to--to--to beer, you know. As I say, I have never been able to hold my liquor when I occasionally take it. The--there is a humorous--one time at Thanksgiving, you know, I heard--I heard the rumor that if--if you--if you didn't finish your--if you took more than you were supposed to, you have to--you are going to have to finish what you took. Either that or you would have to do kitchen police. So I remember stuffing my--one Thanksgiving dinner I took my pockets and stuffed them with cake and then got outside and threw them overboard. Another time that I made a faux pas was that I had to have the 12:00 to 4:00 watch on deck and went into--I had to go to the head. I went down to the wrong room at 2:30 in the morning and turned on the lights in the executive officers' quarters, and for the two weeks after that I had to do KP. But I was afraid that--I think there was one incident that one of the people on the--on the dry dock, the heavy lifts, in other words, they have like a platform if you're going to chip paint, and mostly this is what we did on the dry dock is chip paint. I wasn't--no ships came during that time. But one of--one of--there was a fatality, somebody fell off the lift there. The closest I came to danger was on the way back. After the dry dock was decommissioned, a mine exploded about a mile off the bow of the ship. A couple of amusing incidents. I mean, I was always--was always--I have always been able to wake up early. There was a couple guys at Treasure Island, I guess--TI, Treasury Island? Two names, one was Keela Obshiller (ph) and another is Joe Toomey. And Keela couldn't--when he wakes up he has to sit on the edge of his cot before he could open his eyes, you know, and I was always responsible for waking him up at 7:15 in the morning. Of course, one of the tunes that I remember waking up 6:00 "Hey, Bob a reBob." I think I was introduced--when I was in Dearborn, Michigan, I was introduced to the idea of a Sunday morning breakfast with a big smorgasbord. I mean, before that the breakfast they had was either oatmeal, piece of toast, juice and then milk or something like that. But here they piled on the food. In addition to that, you ate bacon, you ate eggs, you know. A foolish thing, you know, this is basically why I took a test to be in the Navy, because I heard in the Navy they fed you better than the Army. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did it turn out that way, you think?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: I had nothing to compare it to.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Stories of Army food _____?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: It really was--it sounds good, but you had no control to run against.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you assigned to a specific ship?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Yeah. I mean, to, I mean, when I--overseas advance base section dry dock, ABSD No. 5, which was--which was anchored near Samar in the Philippine Islands. That was where I spent most of my--most of my time, and...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you get to the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: It would have to be about--let's see, it would have to be September of '45. And there was a couple of interesting, colorful characters. One there, guy's there named Crawford, the executive officer. Always with a frown on his face. And the rumor was that somehow this gentleman on an--on an expedition of Admiral Byrd--I don't know, I should have looked this up--on either the North or the South Pole, left AWOL, and because of that he was broken to lieutenant commander, he could never rise above that rank, never, you know. That's why at least he always had a frown on his face. And there was also a lieutenant, Lieutenant Underwood, always had kind of a florid complexion. But I don't remember the name of the captain. You didn't see the captain of the ship of the dry dock that much. I also regret I never--I never kept contact with a few people who I spent a little more time with in the Navy than I--than I did. There's Keeva Ovshiller (ph), I guess he was from Atlantic City, New Jersey, and I always wondered what happened to him. But there was a couple other guys, I guess. One of them was Sheldon Perlick and Dave Rush. Sheldon Perlick became a plumbing contractor in this city. I don't think he's living.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now the Philippines were secure at that point, but were they still fighting Japanese on the islands?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Let's see, VJ Day followed pretty fast after VAD. VAD was in June and the other was in August I'm pretty sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. That they dropped bombs in August.

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: And even now I wonder--I almost--you know, I almost wish that in view of the horrible events that are going on today, if America had not dropped the atom bomb, instead had invaded.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news they had dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction, the same at that time then as it is now? Or did you think it was a necessary evil?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: I'm trying to remember. I think at that time I did not have much--I wasn't anywhere as political at that time as I am now . So I did not have firm opinions about that thing, you know. Just in general, I mean, I hate to see the loss of human life, any human life. I mean, I was raised--see, my mother was my more dominant character than my father. For example, when I taught the piano, and I taught the piano for 56 years now. I mean, I've been going to their homes, and now I can't because of this. Because there's always a question, a moral question, do you report all the money, do you report the money you make teaching the piano? And my father said no. My father was an electrician. My mother said yes. Mother understood my idealism. I mean, the idea that I would be able to teach the piano is a beautiful thing, play the piano, a beautiful thing. You don't sully that concept by saying--by lying, you know. And--anyhow...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you think you would have been part of the invasion plans for Japan--

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Yes, I think--I think--in my mind, Tim--

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tom.

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Tom--in my mind, I would have given up my life. I mean, in Hebrew we say two things. "You may not nee lee mere," (ph) if I'm not going to be for myself, who's going to be for me; but "mo shome illee akmee moanee," (ph) if I'm only going to be for myself, what do I long to? And I have always taken the second one and always been for the other guy much more than for myself. Because I feel myself blessed. I mean, I can--I played the Tchaikovsky piano concerto back in 1950. And in my mind I'd give up my life, you know, so that the atom bomb would never--maybe the atom bomb would have been created anyhow. We had research working on it. But the immediacy, you know, the exigency might never have occurred, and then everything that followed, world history, would have been radically changed. It wouldn't be the question now of Saddam Hussein and his massive destruction. It's ridiculous, I mean, the people in this country are suffering. People are going hungry, people killing each other with guns. What the hell do we have to go over in Iraq for? What's his name, wicked, from Russia made a $40 billion deal with Saddam Hussein? What does he know that Bush doesn't know? Anyway, sorry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So even though the projections and speculations were that there would have been a million casualties if they invaded Japan, you--in retrospect, you feel like it would have been the better route to take?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Yeah. I mean, I don't know that--I think Stalin said that--he called it a racist act, they would drop the bomb on the yellow guy, on the gook, rather than the German. And I can't deny that. Just--just--just terrible. We--we--we musicians-- you know, I'm a Jew, but I love my people, but I love all people . What's so special? I mean, we've suffered. All people have suffered. What's so special about the Jewish? Anyhow...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your time in the Navy, does any other particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: No, except when I flunked out. I know I was--I hope I have the privilege of playing the one thing for you that I played when I flunked, the Chopin nocturne if I--if I may before you go. I want to play it for you. I think that was a formative thing, you know, since I flunked out for me it was the hands, I'm not very good, still not very good. Getting around the keys fast has nothing to do with mechanical ability. I helped my father when I went through school, through college. My father was an electrician for Dome Electric. He was a finisher; that is, he put in plugs and switches and fixtures. So I helped him. I mean, I could put in a plug or a switch fast. You just strip a wire, put it in, but that has nothing to do with mechanical ability. My wife is a very good mechanic. Why? Because she's--she's curious. Why doesn't something work? Me, why can't I motivate some kid to play the piano?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you finally get out of the Navy?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Just August of '46. In other words, I was in just under a year and a half. So I was able to get through the GI Bill. I got two-and-a-half years of college. And at that time it was less than $20 a credit hour. So I got a master's degree on the GI Bill of Rights. And that was 36--you could do it with course work, 36 credit hours, and with 78 for the Ph.D., so I got 42--42 credit hours at let's say $15. $15 I had to pay for myself to get the doctorate, which I got in '54. This was before Case Western. It was just Western Reserve University. But...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Are you glad you spent that time in the Navy, though?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Oh, absolutely. I mean, the--absolutely. I mean, at that time I think the GI Bill allowed people from--from the working class, if you will, to rise into the middle class. I mean, my parents, may they rest in peace, lost their house in the Depression of '29. I mean, I had a sister who died from appendicitis at the age of 5. So I was an only child, and I myself never suffered. But they always moved, moved, moved, moved, moved, all the time. I mean, after they lost the house, they rented here, here, here, and finally my mother had to-- parents had to rent from my aunt, my mother's older sister, on Sheldon Road. I have been grateful I have been in the service because, A, I made out okay. I mean, I worked for 44 years. And the great thing about it was, I mean, I retired at age 70. I had a system where at work the volunteer area, nurtured the work area which--it's a constant cycle of--of nurturing. And I would have quit--I would have stayed longer except my wife wasn't in good health, and it wasn't right for me to keep on enjoying while she hurts.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: About the topic, do you have any other memories of the Depression, other than--you know, other than constantly being forced to move?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: No, no, no, no. The memories was--politically I was left wing, I was radical.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: FDR supporter?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Absolutely. I mean, in 1948 after the demise of Henry Wallace I joined the communist party briefly. I understand, you know, when I was growing up on Sheldon Road in my aunt's house, you know, practicing the piano and getting ready to teach, there was some other, one particular girl who wanted to--wanted to play difficult things. She wasn't--she wasn't equipped to do it, and I was always over at the house playing. Her uncle was discussing the Depression. He said the Communist Party was a legitimate party during that period. Talked in terms of maybe a hundred thousand people lost work during that time. And I couldn't hurt a hair on a person's head to carry out what I conceived to be a more just, humane system where everybody owns everything and there's no exploitation, no racism, utopian socialism.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did that cause you any trouble there in the late '40s, early '50s?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: A little bit. I think--I think one time when I was in the library I was reading something that was radical and I think I--someone looked at me, pushed me or something, said you have no desirable character, something like that. But on a whole, no. As a matter of fact, one of the interesting things is in my teaching career I had all kinds of people. One of them was black, and they themselves never experienced racism of any kind. These are intelligent people and quite interesting. One of the interesting things there was a Judge Lloyd Brown, may he rest in peace, a common pleas judge, I think he was appointed by Governor Gilligan. I taught his daughter. They used to live on Seaboard, off Onaway. And I come into the house one time and I--and the judge is at the sink cleaning up the dishes, so I said, "What are you doing here?" And he said, "Well, when my wife comes back, I want her to think I'm a good guy." I would say substantially not. I mean, in my opinion, the--the late Rabbi Rudolph Rosenthal had a temple in the Heights which is now called Civic, used to say if a young person at the age of 18, 19 or 20 isn't a socialist, there's something wrong with them. And if by the time they're 40 years old they haven't gotten rid of the idea, there's also something wrong with them. And meaning, you know, the priority, this person's priority, if it doesn't change so that they are--take a leader of a family and the priorities of the family come first, never mind this other stuff, you know. I understood that. But the--I'm too serious, I know, I know. My wife says I don't have the kind of sense of humor that others do. I don't--I don't laugh so easily. I mean, I cry easily over the--over the state of the world, but I've brought a lot of--a lot of joy into people's houses teaching the piano, a lot of joy, and...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you want to play that for me?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would it be okay if I record it?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's in the other room here, right?

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Give it a try. I'll just put this down here. Practice a little bit. (Piano playing.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. (Piano playing.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wonderful. (Piano playing.)

sp.speaker: Barush Zamesky
sp.p: That's what I call my grateful song, grateful for everything that I have.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was very nice. Thank you. You'll be the first to have played piano on any of these tapes, provide any music. That's great.
